implementation_notes: The dominant .NET answer is a mapping library: a `Profile` subclass registers `CreateMap<User, UserDto>()` in one place, using `ForMember`/`MapFrom`/`Ignore` for the fields that need policy, the container injects `IMapper`, and the boundary calls `_mapper.Map<UserDto>(user)`. Convention mapping does the mechanical copying while the profile remains the single owner of the translation rules - the mapper object of the classic pattern in its configured form. Choose it when many shapes must be mapped and configuration beats hand-written code; keep a hand-written extension method for one-off or hot-path pairs. Mapster is the lighter alternative with the same profile/registration shape, and `AssertConfigurationIsValid` (or equivalent startup validation) is what turns silent name drift into a build-time or startup failure.
pitfalls: Convention mapping hides renames: a property whose name differs becomes a silently default value unless startup validation is enabled.
AutoMapper 9 removed the static API, so injecting IMapper spreads the library through the whole application; keep it inside the boundary assembly.
A profile is configuration without types: renaming a DTO property cannot fail the build, only the validation step or a test.

variants.name: Hand-written mapping over records
variants.implementation_notes: With records and `with` expressions, hand-written mapping is cheap: `public static UserDto ToDto(this User u) => new(u.Id, u.FullName, u.IsAdmin);` plus a matching `ToDomain` keeps both directions in one static class in the boundary assembly, and conversion operators (`implicit operator UserDto(User u)`) or constructors are the alternative form. Choose it for a small, stable pair of shapes, when the mapping needs no configuration, or when a profiler points at the library; positional records then make the compiler keep the mapping honest against field additions, which convention-based mapping does not. Prefer explicit methods over implicit operators at a remote boundary: an implicit conversion that fails throws where the value is used, not where the mapping policy is written.
pitfalls: Implicit conversion operators make translations invisible; a type that converts to three shapes produces ambiguity errors or surprising overload selection.
A hand-written mapper compiles happily when a field is added on one side - only positional record construction or tests catch the omission.
Mapping extension methods on the DTO type drift into the domain assembly if the DTO is shared; keep both in the boundary project.
